issues.issue: The Board is given "exclusive power and authority to exercise the powers set forth in Section 5.5" over self-directed assets, duplicating Section 8.4(b), which states the same rule for assets as to which no Investment Manager has been appointed. The two overlapping grants leave unclear which governs assets an Investment Manager was appointed for but does not in fact manage.

The Board must "meet periodically" with each Investment Manager, a term with no stated interval or benchmark against which compliance could be measured. Section 7.2(13)'s monitoring duty likewise supplies no frequency.

This section makes the fiduciary acknowledgment optional ("may require"), while Section 1.18 makes a written acknowledgment to the Board a defining condition of being an "Investment Manager." Whether a manager without an acknowledgment is an Investment Manager, and thus whether the Board's disclaimers in Sections 8.5 and 8.8 apply to it, cannot be answered from either alone.

The Investment Manager receives the Section 5.5 powers "except subsections (3) through (y)," but Section 5.5 has no subsection numbered (3); its subsections run (a) through (y). The excepted range therefore cannot be identified, leaving the manager's powers indeterminate.

The disclaimer that neither the Board nor the Administrator is "responsible or liable for any acts or omissions of any Investment Manager" cannot be squared with Section 7.2(13)'s duty to "[m]onitor and evaluate" investment managers' performance or Section 7.2(15)'s duty to terminate them where necessary. Whether the Board can be held to those duties despite the disclaimer is a genuine question.

Making the Investment Manager's authority and terms of retention "the sole responsibility of the Board" cannot be squared with Section 8.5, which declares the Board not responsible or liable for any acts or omissions of any Investment Manager, or with Section 8.8's disclaimer. What responsibility the Board retains depends on which provision prevails.

The disclaimer that issuing guidelines is not "an acceptance by the Board of any investment management or supervisory powers" cannot be squared with Section 7.2(10), which requires the Board to formulate and implement general investment policies and to promulgate directions and guidelines. The provision denies the supervisory role another provision imposes.

This section makes the contribution rate governed "at all times" by the Collective Bargaining Agreements and their "amendments, supplements, and modifications," while Section 1.8 recognizes as a Collective Bargaining Agreement only one that "is acceptable to the Board." Whether a side memorandum reapportioning or altering the rate binds the Fund without Board acceptance cannot be answered from either provision alone.

"Amendments, supplements, and modifications" is left undefined, so it is unclear whether letter agreements, memoranda of agreement and reapportionment understandings between an Employer and the Union count as such. The final sentence's promise that nothing here changes "any of the terms or provisions of any such agreement" sharpens the question of what documents are in the set.

Contributions are effective "as of the date specified in the Collective Bargaining Agreement," while Section 2.4(b) makes participation effective on a date the Employer designates. Where the two dates differ, nothing says which governs the obligation to contribute.

The sentence that "[t]he costs and expenses incurred in the collection of Employer contributions shall be paid from the Fund" cannot be squared with Section 9.4(b), Section 9.5(b) and Section 9.7(d), which place those same collection costs, counsel fees and court costs on the delinquent Employer. Who ultimately bears collection costs turns on reconciling them.

The liquidated damage is "the greater of interest on, or twenty percent of, the unpaid contributions," but this subsection states no rate or period for the interest leg of the comparison. Section 9.5(b)'s 18 percent is a rate on "expenses incurred in effectuating such payment," not plainly the measure meant here.

The fixed 18 percent rate is replaced by Amendment No. 2, which adds "or such other interest rate that the Trustees deem appropriate," so the rate referred to by Sections 9.4(a) and 9.7(b) as "the method set forth in Section 9.5" is no longer fixed. Which text applies to a given delinquency period would have to be worked out across the two instruments.

"Several and not joint" is stated without qualification, leaving unclear whether it also disclaims the joint liability of trades or businesses under common control for the contributions and withdrawal liability that Sections 9.6 and 9.10 contemplate under ERISA. The reach of the disclaimer is not fixed by its own words.

The parenthetical "(hereinafter collectively referred to as 'unpaid contributions')" is attached to a list of agreements, rules and guidelines rather than to any sum of money, so the defined term has no coherent antecedent. Section 9.7 then awards "[a]ll unpaid contributions due and payable" in reliance on that defined term.

Interest is to be "computed in accordance with the method set forth in Section 9.5," but Section 9.5(b) states only a flat rate on collection expenses, and as amended leaves the rate to the Trustees' discretion. There is no "method" in Section 9.5 to which this computation can be referred.

This section preserves the right of "the Union, the Plan, the Trust Fund, the Board, or any Committee" to enforce contribution obligations "in any other type of proceeding," while Section 9.10 forbids withdrawal-liability claims from becoming "the subject of litigation in the courts." Which controls a dispute that is both a contribution claim and a withdrawal-liability claim is unresolved.

The Employer must produce "all records deemed necessary by such persons," a scope fixed by the auditor's own judgment with no objective limit, and the Board "may charge an Employer for the cost" without stating any condition such as a finding of underpayment. Both the reach of the audit and the cost-shifting trigger are left undefined.

The mandatory arbitration reaches only "claims by third parties (including Employers) against the Trust Fund concerning the assessment ... of withdrawal liability," leaving open whether an employer's declaratory or contract action about the contribution base, or a claim brought by the Fund, falls within it. The final sentence, preserving the Fund's right to sue in court, deepens the asymmetry.

The proviso that an amendment must not be "inconsistent with the purposes for which the Fund was established" supplies no benchmark, and the purposes are stated differently in the third recital (pension and retirement benefits) and in Section 2.2 (pension and "related" benefits). Whether a given amendment satisfies the proviso cannot be measured from this clause.

The ban on any amendment producing a "return or diversion of any part of the Fund to any of the Contributing Employers" is excepted only "as otherwise provided in Section 10.3," but Section 10.3(b) forbids reversion outright and it is Section 4.4 that authorizes the return of mistaken or nondeductible contributions. The cross-reference points to a provision that grants no exception.

Termination is committed to unanimous Board vote, joint resolution of the Union and the Association, or automatic operation, which cannot be squared with Section 7.2(1)'s statement that the Board has "the right to amend, modify or terminate this Agreement at any time" or Section 4.2's power to terminate the Plan at any time. Who may end the Trust depends on which provision governs.

"Under no circumstances shall any portion of the corpus or income of the Trust Fund ... revert or accrue to the benefit of any Employer" cannot be squared with Section 4.4, which permits the Board to return mistaken, disqualified or nondeductible contributions to the Employer. A refund demand would put the two provisions directly against each other.

The Board's records are made "the official records of the Plan and Trust Fund for all purposes," which sits against Section 9.9, under which an Employer's payroll and wage records are audited to determine the accuracy of contributions. In a contribution dispute the two provisions point to different controlling records.

Valuation is to be at fair market value "computed in accordance with such commercially acceptable valuation method or methods determined by the Board," so the standard is set by the very party whose valuations are at issue and "commercially acceptable" is undefined. Because Section 11.2 governs valuation "[f]or all purposes of this Agreement," the vagueness carries into asset and liability computations.

"The New York City metropolitan area" has no fixed boundary — it is commonly read to include parts of New Jersey and Connecticut — yet the Board "shall be deemed to be located at that address" though no address is given. Situs matters for Section 12.2's choice of law and for venue under Sections 6.6 and 9.10.

The direction that the Agreement "shall not be construed by reference" to titles and headings cannot be squared with Section 1.12, which defines "Corporate Trustee" "as that term is defined in Section 3.12" — a term appearing only in that section's heading, "Use of Corporate Trustee." Giving effect to this section would strip meaning from that definition.

Making "[e]very certificate or other instrument executed by the Chairman of the Trustees" conclusive cannot be squared with Section 5.15, which authorizes execution by "[t]he Chairman and Secretary" or by a resolution-designated pair of Union and Employer Trustees. Whether a third party may rely on the Chairman's signature alone turns on reconciling them.

Importing every word defined in the Plan into this Agreement cannot be squared with Article 1, which independently defines the same key terms ("Plan," "Covered Employee," "Beneficiary," "Employer"), since the Plan is a document the Board may amend unilaterally under Section 4.2. Whether a Plan definition can override an Article 1 definition is left to the words "except as otherwise expressly provided herein."

The addresses and the designation of a "Fund Administrator" here are superseded by Amendment No. 1 and Amendment No. 3, which substitute a "Fund Director" and new addresses. Which notice text is operative for a given communication must be determined across the three instruments.

The provision as printed begins in the middle of a sentence — "the Board) or any person claiming by or through them" — with no subject identifying whose rights are being denied. As written, the class of persons who "shall [not] have any right, title or interest" cannot be determined from the section.

The disclaimer of "any equity or other interest in the assets of the Fund, except as set forth in the Plan" sits against Section 12.15, under which no person has any right to a benefit "unless and until the Board determines" the requirements are met. Whether a Plan-conferred interest exists before a Board determination is unresolved between them.

The amendment substitutes for a fixed 18 percent "such other interest rate that the Trustees deem appropriate given [the] circumstance[s]," a standard with no cap, floor or benchmark, set by the party collecting. Sections 9.4(a) and 9.7(b), which compute interest "in accordance with" Section 9.5, are left without an ascertainable rate.

The closing sentence reads "The appointment of Trustees shall be selected by the provisions of Section 3.4," a mechanical error for "governed by" that leaves the appointment rule stated ungrammatically and in doubt. Section 3.4 in any event addresses only written appointments and acceptances of successors.

Providing that the Union Trustees "shall be" the incumbent president and vice president/secretary-treasurer cannot be squared with amended Section 3.1's grant to the Union of the power to select its two Trustees, or with Section 3.10, under which the principal officer designates a successor. Whether an office-holder automatically becomes a Trustee is left unresolved among these provisions.
